title: Validating references with lifetimes
summary: Dangling references and the borrow checker, lifetime annotations in functions, what 'a really promises, lifetimes in structs, the three elision rules, 'static, and combining lifetimes with generics.

sections: TRPL 10.3 Generic Type Parameters, Trait Bounds, and Lifetimes
CR Day 3 Lifetimes in Data Structures

blocks.md:
Every reference has a **lifetime**: the part of the program during which it is valid. Most of the time lifetimes are inferred, just as most types are. Occasionally the compiler cannot work out how the lifetimes of several references relate, and you must tell it with **lifetime annotations**. They never change how long anything lives; they only **describe** relationships so the compiler can check them.

The purpose is to prevent **dangling references**: a reference to data that no longer exists.

blocks.explain: `x` is dropped at the inner `}`, but `r` is still used after it. The **borrow checker** compares scopes: the reference's lifetime must not outlast the data it points to.

blocks.title: When the compiler needs help
blocks.md: Here is a function that returns the longer of two string slices:

blocks.output:
error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
 --> src/main.rs:1:33
  |
1 | fn longest(x: &str, y: &str) -> &str {
  |               ----     ----     ^ expected named lifetime parameter
  |
  = help: this function's return type contains a borrowed value, but the signature does not say whether it is borrowed from `x` or `y`
help: consider introducing a named lifetime parameter
  |
1 | fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str {
  |           ++++     ++          ++          ++
blocks.explain: The returned reference comes from `x` or from `y`, decided at run time. The caller needs to know how long the result stays valid, and the compiler checks each function by its signature alone, so the signature must say it.

blocks.title: Lifetime annotation syntax

blocks.explain: You can see that `result` would point to `string1`, which is still alive. The compiler cannot: by the signature, the result may borrow from `string2`, which is dropped at the `}`. Move the `println!` inside the inner block and it compiles.

blocks.title: Annotations describe; they do not extend
blocks.md: Writing `'a` does not make any value live longer. It states a relationship ("the output borrows from these inputs") that the compiler then enforces at every call. If a parameter has nothing to do with the result, leave it out: `fn first<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &str) -> &'a str` returns `x` and lets `y` have any lifetime.

A function cannot return a reference to a value it created itself, whatever the annotations say, because that value is dropped when the function returns. Return an owned value instead:

```rust
fn make() -> String {          // not -> &str
    String::from("really long string")
}
```

blocks.title: Lifetimes in structs
blocks.md: A struct may hold references, but then every reference field needs a lifetime, declared on the struct. The annotation means "an instance of this struct cannot outlive the data it borrows":

blocks.title: Lifetime elision
blocks.md: Early Rust required annotations on every reference in a signature. The common patterns were so predictable that the compiler now fills them in using three **elision rules**. If the rules leave an output lifetime undecided, you get error E0106 and must annotate.

steps.title: Rule 1: each input reference gets its own lifetime
steps.md: `fn f(x: &str, y: &str)` is read as `fn f<'a, 'b>(x: &'a str, y: &'b str)`.

steps.title: Rule 2: one input lifetime is given to all outputs
steps.md: With exactly one input lifetime, the output must borrow from it. `first_word` is now complete; no annotation needed.

steps.title: Rule 3: in methods, outputs get self's lifetime
steps.md: If one input is `&self` or `&mut self`, its lifetime goes to all outputs. That is why `announce_and_return_part(&self, announcement: &str) -> &str` compiled: the result borrows from `self`.

steps.title: longest is left undecided
steps.md: Two input lifetimes, no `self`: rule 2 and rule 3 do not apply, the output has no lifetime, and you must write `'a`.
steps.code: fn longest<'a, 'b>(x: &'a str, y: &'b str) -> &str   // ??? -> E0106

blocks.title: The 'static lifetime
blocks.md: `'static` means "can live for the whole program". All string literals are `&'static str`, because their text is stored in the program's binary. When the compiler suggests adding `'static`, it is usually wrong advice for your situation: the real fix is generally an owned value or a correct relationship between lifetimes. `T: 'static` as a bound (common with threads) means "T holds no short-lived references"; owned types such as `String` satisfy it.

blocks.title: Borrowing parsers
blocks.goal: Write functions and a struct that return and hold references into their input, with correct lifetime annotations.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub fn longest_word<'a>(text: &'a str) -> &'a str`: the longest whitespace-separated word (the first on a tie), or `""` for no words. (Elision would work here; write it out.)
- `pub fn longer_of<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str`: the longer string, `a` on a tie.
- `pub fn after_prefix<'a>(text: &'a str, prefix: &str) -> Option<&'a str>`: the part after `prefix` if `text` starts with it. The prefix must **not** be tied to the result.
- `pub struct Tokens<'a> { rest: &'a str }` with `pub fn new(text: &'a str) -> Self` and `pub fn next_token(&mut self) -> Option<&'a str>`, returning the next comma-separated piece, trimmed, until the text is used up. Empty pieces are skipped.
hints: `text.split_whitespace()` yields words; keep one when `w.len() > best.len()`.
In `next_token`: loop; if `rest` is empty return `None`; split with `match self.rest.split_once(',')`, set `self.rest` to the remainder, trim the piece, and return it if non-empty.
The return type is `Option<&'a str>`, not `Option<&str>`: the token borrows from the original text, not from `self`. That lets callers keep tokens while calling `next_token` again.
blocks.solution_explain: `next_token` returns `Option<&'a str>`: tokens borrow from the original text, not from the `Tokens` value. With the elided `Option<&str>` they would borrow from `&mut self` (rule 3), and the last test could not hold `first` while calling `next_token` again. This is the same design as the standard library's `split` iterators.

points: A lifetime is the span during which a reference is valid; the borrow checker rejects references that would outlive their data.
Annotations like `'a` relate the lifetimes of inputs and outputs; they never change how long values live.
Structs holding references need lifetime parameters and cannot outlive what they borrow.
Elision rules: each input gets a lifetime; a single input lifetime goes to outputs; in methods, `self`'s lifetime goes to outputs.
`'static` lives for the whole program; string literals have it. It is rarely the right fix for a lifetime error.

terms.def: The region of code during which a reference is guaranteed to be valid.
A name like 'a that relates the lifetimes of references in a signature or struct.
The part of the compiler that checks every borrow is valid for as long as it is used.
Rules that let the compiler infer lifetimes in common signatures so you need not write them.
The lifetime of the entire program run; string literals have it.
A reference to memory that has been freed; Rust rejects these at compile time.
